atoms.text: The survivor's payout: subscribers pool money and each death increases the income of those still alive, so longevity is rewarded by other people's deaths.
The mortality lottery: participants cannot know when they will die, so the scheme converts a shared fate into a competition.
The last survivor: the final member inherits the remaining fund, so the story's ending is a waiting game with a single winner.
The group annuity: strangers become financially entangled for life, so solidarity is also a stake in each other's deaths.
The suspicious accident: a tontine gives every survivor a motive to hasten a death, so actuarial math becomes a murder map.
The government scheme: a state raises capital by promising lifetime incomes, so public finance bets on citizens' lifespans.
The scandal: abuses lead to investigation and restriction, so a financial instrument becomes a moral panic.
The elderly subscriber: an old person's payout rises as friends die, so prosperity is built from grief.
The trust that cannot be exited: members cannot withdraw without losing their stake, so commitment is total.
The named beneficiary: the fund is linked to a specific living person, so a body becomes collateral.
The revival: a discredited scheme returns as a retirement product, so old exploitation is rebranded as innovation.
The actuary who knows the odds: an expert can estimate who will die first, so knowledge is power over the group.
The birthday clause: a subscriber must survive to a date to collect, so a calendar becomes a threat.
The closed circle: new members cannot join once the scheme starts, so the group becomes a sealed society.
The final death: the trust winds up when the last member dies, so the scheme's end is also its purpose.
The shared risk: members pool the danger of living too long, so the story can frame mutual aid as mutual hostage-taking.
